teaser.text: GSK plc is a British company that develops, makes and sells prescription medicines and vaccines. Its business is a loop: products already on sale bring in money, and that money pays for supply, research and the next generation of products.

blocks.heading: What has to go right for GSK, and what could go wrong?

paragraphs.text: Base earnings rise to £7,565m in the first forecast year and £7,725m in the second. They reach £7,826m in the third. The underlying case assumes modest revenue growth and slightly lower normalized margins as mature products weaken. This is below management’s ambition of more than £40bn of risk-adjusted sales in 2031, because analyst consensus is £36.446bn.

The bear case falls from £7,148m to £6,960m and then £6,508m. It assumes weak replacement sales and faster HIV erosion. The bull case rises from £7,700m to £8,140m and then £8,550m, assuming launches gain patients, vaccines remain strong and savings improve operating leverage.

blocks.heading: How much cash does GSK really make?

paragraphs.text: Cash from operations was £7,741 million in 2025. After capital spending, lease payments and interest, the free-cash-flow measure used here was £3,836 million. Deducting stock-based pay produces “real free cash flow” of £3,462 million, because shares given to employees still dilute owners even though they are not a current cash payment.

blocks.heading: How much does GSK pay per share over time?

paragraphs.text: GSK also returned capital through a £2 billion buyback completed in June 2026 and expected a 70p dividend for 2026. Those actions reduce the shares or cash available for future investment, so their value depends on the price paid and the opportunities forgone. GSK recycled other assets too: it retained a 78.3% economic interest in ViiV and received a $250 million special dividend, while licensing linerixibat generated $400 million upfront. Such proceeds support cash flow, but gains from disposals are not the same as recurring medicine sales. The final test is what this focused portfolio can earn.

The base dividend is £0.70 per share initially and £0.72 in the second year. It reaches £0.74 in the third, consistent with progressive policy but limited by investment needs. The bear case cuts it to £0.66 and then £0.60; the bull case raises it to £0.74 and then £0.78.

blocks.heading: Does GSK’s cash cover its dividend?

paragraphs.text: Revenue rose across the five-year period, with the 2022 jump shaped by the Haleon demerger and continuing-business presentation. Operating margin recovered in 2025 after the 2024 fall; reported and Core profit separate selected charges, and real free cash flow as a share of revenue, after investment and stock pay, recovered too. GSK’s own real free cash flow per share was 84.09p against diluted EPS of 138.80p. Shareholder distributions exceeded that cash measure.

Cash from operations was £7,741 million in 2025. After capital spending, lease payments and interest, the free-cash-flow measure used here was £3,836 million. Deducting stock-based pay produces “real free cash flow” of £3,462 million, because shares given to employees still dilute owners even though they are not a current cash payment.

paragraphs.text: The main risk is loss of exclusivity, when cheaper generic competitors can enter after a medicine’s protection ends. GSK expects this period for dolutegravir in 2028–2030. Its savings programme targets £1.9bn annually by 2029, but much of the money is intended to fund replacement medicines rather than become dividends.

earnings.title: GSK earnings: October 28, 2026 results
earnings.meta_description: GSK reports on October 28, 2026; guidance is 3.0%–5.0% turnover growth and 7.0%–9.0% core profit and EPS growth.
earnings.opening: GSK’s next results are expected on October 28, 2026. Watch whether approvals become sales while restructuring improves cash generation without weakening research.
earnings.closing: The full memo also covers GSK’s business, rivals, management and risks.

paragraphs.text: Management reaffirmed 2026 turnover growth of 3.0%–5.0% and core operating-profit and earnings-per-share growth of 7.0%–9.0%. “Core” is GSK’s view of ordinary trading after removing major restructuring, acquisition, impairment and legal items. Those costs still consume cash: in Q2 2026, total operating profit fell 75% while core operating profit rose 7%.

blocks.heading: Has GSK kept its past promises?

paragraphs.text: GSK first guided to sales growth of 3%–5% for 2025. It guided to core operating profit growth of 6%–8%. It delivered 7% sales growth and 11% core operating profit growth, exceeding those initial ranges. That supports the record of promises kept, although Miels’ newer savings promises remain untested.

blocks.heading: What do GSK’s last eight reported periods show?

paragraphs.text: Revenue rose to £8,409 million from £7,986 million a year earlier, while gross margin edged up to 73.1%. Operating income nevertheless fell to £481 million, and diluted EPS fell to 10.70p. Sales and production economics therefore held up while costs below gross profit deteriorated.

blocks.heading: What should GSK watch in the next release?

paragraphs.text: GSK reports Q3 on 28 October 2026. Investors will want to see whether trials have begun, how much restructuring cash has been paid, and whether sales and core profit remain consistent with guidance. The separate currency effect on Q3 sales will help distinguish commercial performance from translation into pounds.

Two regulatory dates make the autumn important. The US regulator’s action date for bepirovirsen is 26 October, while neladalkib’s target date is 27 November. An action date is a target for a regulatory decision, not a promise of approval. Japan approved bepirovirsen as Hibsago on 24 August, but GSK still needs eligible patients, supply and reimbursement to turn approval into treatment.
